sentences: The city museum is free to visit.
It attracts many school groups.
drills.hint: Put the extra fact about the museum between two commas, starting with "which".

sentences: Solar power produces no direct emissions.
It is becoming cheaper.
drills.hint: "Which" describes a thing; the extra clause sits between two commas.

sentences: The Amazon rainforest is shrinking.
It is home to many species.
drills.hint: A non-defining clause adds extra information and needs a comma on both sides.

sentences: The city's metro system is very cheap for students.
It carries many commuters.
drills.hint: Use "which" for a thing; put the extra detail straight after the noun.

sentences: Smartphones are now essential for many students.
They were once a luxury.
drills.hint: The relative clause goes right after "Smartphones", with a comma on each side.

sentences: The new sports centre has a large pool.
It opened in the spring.
drills.hint: Add the extra information about the building between commas, then finish the main clause.

sentences: Fast food is cheap and convenient.
It is often high in salt.
drills.hint: Put the extra fact between commas after the subject, then give the main verb.

sentences: English is taught in most schools.
It is a global language.
drills.hint: A comma before "which" shows the clause is extra information about English.

sentences: Online banking saves customers a lot of time.
It was rare twenty years ago.
drills.hint: Use "which", not a time word, because the clause describes the service itself.

sentences: The recycling scheme was launched last year.
It has already reduced waste.
drills.hint: Subject, then the "which" clause between commas, then the main verb.

sentences: The old town attracts millions of tourists.
It was built in medieval times.
drills.hint: "Which" is the subject of "was built", so you cannot use a place word here.

sentences: The study took two years.
Hundreds of adults took part in it.
drills.hint: Formal style moves the preposition "in" before "which".

sentences: Many people now work from home.
This has reduced rush-hour traffic.
drills.hint: Use a comma and "which" to refer back to the whole first idea.

sentences: The bus fare was cut by half.
This encouraged more people to use buses.
drills.hint: "Which" after a comma can refer to a whole clause; "that" never follows a comma.

sentences: The factory closed last year.
This led to many job losses.
drills.hint: "Which" here refers to the whole event, so put a comma before it.

sentences: Some schools have banned mobile phones.
This has improved concentration in class.
drills.hint: "Which" refers to the whole ban, so the verb after it is singular.

sentences: Food prices rose sharply last winter.
This hit poorer families hardest.
drills.hint: Replace "This" with "which" after a comma to join the result to the event.

sentences: Many graduates move abroad for work.
This creates skill shortages at home.
drills.hint: "Which" refers to the whole situation, not to the graduates, so the verb is singular.

sentences: The council planted trees along the main road.
This has made the area cooler in summer.
drills.hint: Finish the first idea, add a comma, then use "which" for its effect.

sentences: The hospital extended its opening hours.
This has shortened waiting times.
drills.hint: "Which" after a comma sums up the whole first clause.

sentences: Many families now eat out regularly.
This has changed traditional eating habits.
drills.hint: Put a comma before "which" when it refers to a whole idea.

sentences: The company introduced flexible hours.
This made its staff much happier.
drills.hint: "What" cannot follow a comma to refer back; use the relative pronoun for a whole clause.

sentences: Fewer students are choosing science degrees.
This worries many employers.
drills.hint: When "which" refers to a whole idea, the verb after it is singular.

sentences: Life expectancy has risen in many countries.
This puts pressure on pension systems.
drills.hint: Only one relative word can follow a comma and refer to a whole clause.

sentences: Some students work part-time.
They often have less time to study.
drills.hint: No commas: the clause tells us which students we mean.

sentences: Some people exercise regularly.
They tend to sleep better.
drills.hint: Use "who" for people; no commas because it says which people you mean.

sentences: Some drivers use their phones while driving.
They put others at risk.
drills.hint: The "who" clause identifies the drivers, so it takes no commas.

sentences: Some children read every day.
They usually have a wider vocabulary.
drills.hint: "Who" is the subject of "read", so the subject form is needed.

sentences: Some tourists respect local customs.
They are usually welcomed warmly.
drills.hint: Put the defining clause straight after "Tourists", then the main verb.

sentences: Some employees feel valued.
They are more productive.
drills.hint: A defining clause after a person needs "who" and no commas.

sentences: My grandmother lives alone in the countryside.
She is eighty-five years old.
drills.hint: There is only one grandmother, so the extra fact goes between commas.

sentences: Dr Patel is a marine biologist.
She gave a talk at our school.
drills.hint: After a name, add extra information with commas on both sides.

sentences: Some older people use the internet.
They tend to feel less isolated.
drills.hint: No commas: the clause limits the meaning to one group of older people.

sentences: Some workers lose their jobs to automation.
They need to be retrained.
drills.hint: The "who" clause comes between the subject and its verb.

sentences: Our head teacher is retiring this year.
She has worked here for decades.
drills.hint: We know which head teacher, so the extra clause takes commas.

sentences: The local volunteers clean the beach every month.
They are mostly retired people.
drills.hint: Put the extra detail about the volunteers between commas.

sentences: Some patients miss their appointments.
They have to wait longer for treatment.
drills.hint: The defining clause tells us which patients; do not use commas.

sentences: The author grew up in poverty.
She now funds free libraries.
drills.hint: "Who" is the subject of "grew up", so the object form is wrong here.

sentences: The professor retired last year.
Many students admired her.
drills.hint: Use "whom" when the person is the object of the verb in the clause.

sentences: The manager is very experienced.
We interviewed him yesterday.
drills.hint: The manager is the object of "interviewed", so use the formal object pronoun.

sentences: The volunteers were thanked by the mayor.
We owe them a great deal.
drills.hint: In formal English the preposition goes before "whom".

sentences: The athletes were all under twenty.
The coach selected them.
drills.hint: "Whom" is the object of "selected"; no commas in a defining clause.

sentences: The candidate has strong leadership skills.
The panel chose her.
drills.hint: The candidate is the object of "chose", so use the formal object pronoun.

sentences: The tutor is very patient.
I work with her every week.
drills.hint: Formal style puts "with" before the relative pronoun for people.

sentences: Some children's parents read to them.
These children often enjoy reading.
drills.hint: "Whose" shows possession: the parents belong to the children.

sentences: The company is growing fast.
Its products are sold online.
drills.hint: Replace "Its" with "whose" to show the products belong to the company.

sentences: My neighbour is a nurse at the local hospital.
Her son studies medicine.
drills.hint: Replace "Her" with the possessive relative pronoun.

sentences: Some workers' jobs are at risk.
They should learn new skills.
drills.hint: "Whose" + noun tells us which workers; no commas are needed.

sentences: The village is attracting new residents.
Its school was saved from closure.
drills.hint: "Whose" can show possession for places and things as well as people.

sentences: Some cities have poor public transport.
Their roads are usually congested.
drills.hint: Use the possessive relative word before "public transport"; no commas.

sentences: The scientist won a major award.
Her work focuses on clean water.
drills.hint: Replace "Her" with "whose" and put the clause between commas.

sentences: Some patients' symptoms are mild.
They can be treated at home.
drills.hint: "Whose" links the patients to their symptoms; no commas are needed.

sentences: The festival is popular with families.
Its main events are free.
drills.hint: Replace "Its" with the possessive relative pronoun.

sentences: Some countries' populations are ageing.
They face rising health costs.
drills.hint: "Whose" + noun defines which countries we mean, so no commas.

sentences: The firm was criticised by customers.
Its prices rose without warning.
drills.hint: The prices belong to the firm, so a possessive relative word is needed.

sentences: The architect designed the new library.
Her work uses recycled materials.
drills.hint: Put the possessive clause straight after "The architect", between commas.

sentences: I grew up in a small village.
There was no secondary school there.
drills.hint: Use "where" for a place when a full clause follows.

sentences: The park is very popular.
Families have picnics there.
drills.hint: "Where" replaces "there" and refers to a place.

sentences: The library has a quiet room.
Students can study there.
drills.hint: "Where" means "in which" and refers back to the room.

sentences: We visited a factory.
Cars are made there.
drills.hint: Use the place word because "there" in the second sentence refers to the factory.

sentences: Many people move to cities.
There are more jobs in cities.
drills.hint: Use "where" after a comma to add information about a place.

sentences: The hotel is close to the beach.
We stayed there last summer.
drills.hint: "Stay" needs "in" or "at" with "which", so use the place word.

sentences: Some countries offer free university education.
Student debt is low in these countries.
drills.hint: Put the place first, then "where" and a full clause about it.

sentences: The hospital has opened a new ward.
Elderly patients can recover there.
drills.hint: "Where" refers to the ward as a place.

sentences: Many firms have open-plan offices.
Staff find it hard to concentrate there.
drills.hint: Replace "there" with a relative word for places.

sentences: The region is famous for its vineyards.
Tourism has grown quickly there.
drills.hint: Add the extra fact about the region between commas.

sentences: Young people are leaving the coastal town.
There are few jobs there.
drills.hint: The second sentence describes the town, a place, so use the place word.

sentences: Researchers studied schools in rural areas.
Internet access is often poor there.
drills.hint: "Where" refers back to the rural areas; a full clause follows it.

sentences: I will never forget the day.
I passed my driving test that day.
drills.hint: Use "when" after a noun of time such as "day".

sentences: Traffic is worst in the morning.
Most people travel to work then.
drills.hint: "When" replaces "then" and refers to a time.

sentences: Shops are busy in December.
People buy gifts for the holidays then.
drills.hint: Add a comma after the time phrase, then the time relative word.

sentences: My grandparents grew up in the 1950s.
Few families owned a television then.
drills.hint: "When" adds information about a period of time.

sentences: Exams take place in June.
Students feel most stressed then.
drills.hint: Use the time word after "June" and a comma.

sentences: Electricity costs more in the evening.
Demand is at its highest then.
drills.hint: "When" refers back to the evening, a time.

sentences: The museum is free on Sundays.
Most families visit then.
drills.hint: Use the time relative word after "Sundays" and a comma.

sentences: Travel was expensive in the past.
Few people went abroad then.
drills.hint: "Then" in the second sentence becomes a relative word for time.

sentences: Retirement is a stage of life.
Many people take up new hobbies then.
drills.hint: A stage of life is a time, so use the time word with no comma.

sentences: Unemployment rose during the recession.
Many firms stopped hiring then.
drills.hint: "When" adds extra information about the period of the recession.

sentences: Some foods contain a lot of sugar.
They can damage teeth.
drills.hint: Use "that" with no commas to say which foods you mean.

sentences: Some cars run on electricity.
They produce less pollution.
drills.hint: "That" introduces a defining clause about things; do not use commas.

sentences: I bought a laptop.
It has a long battery life.
drills.hint: Put the defining clause straight after the thing it describes.

sentences: Some jobs require a degree.
They usually pay more.
drills.hint: "That" tells us which jobs; the main verb comes after the clause.

sentences: The city has a law.
It bans cars from the centre.
drills.hint: "That" replaces "It" and refers back to the law.

sentences: Some apps track sleep.
They can help users rest better.
drills.hint: A defining clause about things can begin with "that"; no commas.

sentences: Some buildings use solar panels.
They have lower energy bills.
drills.hint: The clause identifies the buildings, so it needs no commas.

sentences: The government passed a law.
It protects ancient forests.
drills.hint: Join the second idea to "a law" with a relative word for things.

sentences: Some diseases spread through water.
They are common in poorer regions.
drills.hint: Subject, defining clause, then the main verb; no commas.

sentences: Some films are based on true stories.
They often attract large audiences.
drills.hint: "That" refers to things and defines which films we mean.

sentences: The report suggests changes.
These changes could reduce crime.
drills.hint: The relative clause comes right after "changes".

sentences: Some products are made locally.
They have a smaller carbon footprint.
drills.hint: Put the defining clause between the subject and the main verb.

sentences: Many students choose courses.
These courses lead directly to jobs.
drills.hint: "That" replaces "These courses" and follows the noun directly.

sentences: Employers value certain skills.
These skills are rarely taught in school.
drills.hint: Here "that" is the object of "value"; the main verb comes after the clause.

sentences: The city has many parks.
Most of them are free to enter.
drills.hint: Use "most of which" for things; "them" would create two sentences joined by a comma.

sentences: The survey questioned hundreds of teenagers.
Many of them use social media daily.
drills.hint: After a comma, use "of whom" for people.

sentences: The company employs many young people.
Some of them work remotely.
drills.hint: After "of", the object form is needed for people.

sentences: The museum owns thousands of paintings.
Few of them are on display.
drills.hint: Paintings are things, so use "of which" after the comma.

sentences: The town has three schools.
All of them achieve good results.
drills.hint: "All of which" joins the clauses; a plain pronoun would make a comma splice.

sentences: The scheme helped thousands of families.
Many of them had low incomes.
drills.hint: Families are people, so use "of whom" after the comma.

sentences: The rainforest contains countless plants.
Some of them are used in medicine.
drills.hint: Plants are things, so use "of which" after the comma.

sentences: The hospital employs hundreds of nurses.
Many of them work night shifts.
drills.hint: Use "of whom" for people after a comma; "them" cannot join two clauses.
